methods.label: Areas and a cost-saving exchange
methods.explanation:
Because Rose plants one flower per square foot, each region's area is also its number of flowers. Multiplying the labeled side lengths, the upper-left, upper-right, lower-right, and bottom-left regions have areas
\[
4\cdot5=20,\quad 7\cdot3=21,\quad
5\cdot3=15,\quad 6\cdot1=6.
\]
The central rectangle has width \(6-4=2\) and height \(5-3=2\), so its area is \(4\) square feet.

To minimize cost, larger regions should receive cheaper flowers. To justify this, suppose a larger region has a more expensive type than a smaller region. Pair each flower in the smaller region with one flower in the larger region. Swapping the two types leaves each pair's combined cost unchanged, while every unpaired flower in the larger region becomes cheaper. Thus the swap reduces the total cost.

Consequently, a minimum must assign increasing prices to decreasing areas. Assign asters, begonias, cannas, dahlias, and Easter lilies to the regions of areas \(21,20,15,6,4\), respectively. This uses each type once and gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{cost}&=21(1)+20(1.50)+15(2)\\
&\quad+6(2.50)+4(3)\\
&=108.
\end{aligned}
\]
The least possible cost is \(\boxed{108}\) dollars, choice A.
